job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a design engineer at a pump manufacturer in Zaragoza. I studied mechanical engineering, and my final project was a cooling jacket for a small electric motor. Most days I redraw parts in CAD after the factory floor sends back notes, and I eat lunch with Pilar, who's worked there for twenty-six years and teaches me where the drawings lie.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that the work is solid, a pump either works or it doesn't. What wears me out is the commute, the loan and the fact that I earn so little. I rent a room with a roommate, I've got about ten days of spending in the bank, and my parents can't help because my father's work has been short for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it's what I'd expect. I don't use AI tools at work and I wouldn't start. If a program saves a few minutes on drawings then fine, but the pumps still have to be designed by someone who understands water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still nervous, but not about AI. It's the money. I owe a lot, I can't save, and there aren't many engineering firms near Zaragoza, so if this one had a bad year I'd have nowhere to go without moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: do my work, learn the older drawings from Pilar and take every hour of overtime they offer. I'd keep 40 a month aside, cut out my coffee on the way to work and try to renew my contract before it's due. I'd talk to my father about the family plan if work stayed slow for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in a low steady way. Not afraid, just aware that I'm one bad month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your contract is due. When?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In April. It's a one-year graduate contract, and they usually offer a permanent one to about half of us. I don't know yet which half I'm in, and I don't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in my family you don't push for things. You work hard and wait to be noticed. My father always said asking makes you look needy, though I know the quiet ones are sometimes passed over.

say: AI is not **my business**, since pumps still need someone who understands water.
I'd tell friends things will carry on as usual.
think: My worry is the **money**, not AI, because I'm one bad month from trouble.
Few engineering firms are near Zaragoza, so I'd have **nowhere to go**.
do: Take every **overtime** hour the firm offers.
Set aside **40 a month** and skip the daily coffee.
Learn the older drawings from Pilar before my contract is due in April.
feel: **Low steady worry**, aware I'm one bad month from trouble.
S0.quote: In my family you don't push for things. You work hard and wait to be noticed. My father always said asking makes you look needy
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from **debt** and a short contract, not AI.
Doesn't ask for security because of how she was raised.
Learns from an older colleague, which suits her habits.

steps.text: Work every overtime hour offered until the contract is renewed
Put 40 a month into a separate account
Stop buying coffee on the way to work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise, but I'd be honest that some jobs will change. I'd tell friends who write code that they should be careful. For me, I'd say a pump factory is a pump factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not as safe as I say. Redrawing parts and checking dimensions is thinking work, and if the CAD program starts doing it, one designer does the work of three. The first people the firm wouldn't replace are the ones on contracts, like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder to be useful on the factory floor, doing things a screen can't, like watching a test and reading a vibration. I'd ask Pilar to teach me what she knows, since that knowledge isn't written anywhere. I'd still not use the AI tools, but I'd keep my eyes open about what they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. Like hearing a noise in the engine and not knowing if it's serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the tools. Why keep that stance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust what I don't understand. I'd rather make a slow drawing I can defend than a quick one I can't explain, and I know that's old-fashioned for twenty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your manager asks you to use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn, because I'd have to. I'd go slowly and check every result by hand, and I'd tell the manager that's why I'm slower.

say: It's mostly **noise**, though some jobs will change, and coders should be careful.
A pump factory is still a pump factory.
think: Redrawing parts is **thinking work**, so one designer could do the work of three.
Contract staff like me would be the **first** the firm doesn't replace.
do: Spend more time on the **factory floor**, watching tests and reading vibration.
Ask **Pilar** to teach me what isn't written down.
Keep my eyes open about what the AI tools do without using them.
feel: **Uneasy**, like hearing a noise in the engine without knowing if it's serious.
S1.quote: I'd rather make a slow drawing I can defend than a quick one I can't explain
fieldNote: She says one thing publicly and fears another; **contract staff** are exposed.
Resistance to AI comes from distrust, not ignorance.
Plans to rely on tacit knowledge no one has written down.

steps.text: Spend two afternoons a week on the factory floor with Pilar
Keep drawing by hand-checked CAD and not use AI tools
Watch how the firm treats other contract staff before deciding anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is far too fast for a normal person, and I wouldn't joke about it. I'd tell my friends to hold on to what they have and not take new debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think my job goes within a year or two. A design engineer on a short contract is easy to replace with a thinking machine, and robots arriving in 2031 would make factory floors hollow soon after. I'd have a loan and no field to go back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything except rent, food and the loan. I'd ask my parents if I could move home for a while, which is hard since my father's work is short, but it's family. I'd register for any government programme I could find and talk to the town council about retraining for local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I think of Pilar and the others who've been there twenty years and have mortgages, and it makes my chest tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving home is hard. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet. My mother would say of course, and my father would leave the room. We don't talk about money, so no one would say it, but we'd all feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that rush it, and the governments that let them. I'm not angry at the machines. It's the people who decided two years was fine.

say: Two years is **far too fast**, and I'd tell friends to avoid new debts.
think: A short-contract designer is **easy to replace**, and factory floors empty after 2031.
I'd have a loan and **no field** to go back to.
do: Spend only on **rent, food** and the loan.
Ask my parents if I can **move home** for a while.
Register for **government programmes** and ask the council about retraining.
feel: **Frightened**, thinking of colleagues with mortgages, and my chest feels tight.
S2.quote: I'm not angry at the machines. It's the people who decided two years was fine.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and moves to family and state help.
Family silence about money shows what asking costs her.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent, food and loan payments
Move back to my parents' house for a few months
Register for every government retraining programme in the region
Talk to the town council about local jobs and training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, and people should take it seriously. I wouldn't change my own plans overnight, though. I'd tell friends to keep their jobs and pay down debt while they still can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I have two or three years to find something sturdier. Design work will go early, so I'd want to be nearer to the factory floor, or somewhere a person must stand, like maintenance or testing. I wouldn't feel safe in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to move me into the test lab, which is half hands-on. I'd pay the loan down as fast as possible, even if I had to live on beans. And I'd ask Pilar, who's near retirement, to train me before she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. But I can think about it clearly, which I couldn't do with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maintenance and testing. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a machine can say a pump is failing, but someone has to go and listen to it. Robots for hands-on work arrive three years later, so those jobs should last longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about leaving the design office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss it, but I'm not attached to a chair. I'm attached to being employed.

say: Five years is **short**, and people should keep jobs and pay down debt.
think: I have **two or three years** to find something sturdier than design work.
I wouldn't feel safe **in the office**.
do: Ask the firm to move me into the **test lab**, which is half hands-on.
Pay the **loan** down as fast as possible.
Ask Pilar to **train me** before she retires.
feel: **Still anxious**, but I can think clearly, which two years wouldn't allow.
S3.quote: I'm not attached to a chair. I'm attached to being employed.
fieldNote: A few years lets her think clearly about a **hands-on move**.

steps.text: Ask my manager for a move to the test lab
Put every overtime payment toward the loan
Learn pump testing and vibration reading from Pilar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time, and I'd say people are over-worrying. I'd tell friends that a lot can change in ten years, including the date on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see ten years as a chance to get my life in order. I'd be 32, married maybe, in a home of my own, and well out of debt. But I'd still be careful, because the card says the end point is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm, get the permanent contract and then pay off the loan within six years. I'd study for the engineers' chartered qualification in the evenings, since it proves what you can do. I'd save for a small flat in Zaragoza and ask my parents how they might use my help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not calm, but okay. I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be careful because the end point is the same. What does careful look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not borrowing for anything silly, and not tying everything to one firm. I'd keep two skills going, design and testing, so I'm not stuck if one shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have by the halfway point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan down by half, a permanent job and some money in the bank that's my own. That's a modest list, but it's where I'm starting from.

say: Ten years is long, and **a lot can change**, including the date on the card.
think: Ten years is a chance to get my **life in order**, with my debt gone.
I'd still be careful because the **end point** is the same.
do: Get the **permanent contract** and clear the loan within six years.
Study for the **chartered qualification** in the evenings.
Save for a small **flat** in Zaragoza.
S4.quote: I'd keep two skills going, design and testing, so I'm not stuck if one shrinks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd have no savings, a loan and no time, and my parents have little to give. What would help is real notice from companies and a government plan that doesn't make me beg for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that quiet people like me have opinions too. We don't post them, but we're thinking about this every day.

headlineQuote: Quiet people like me have opinions too. We don't post them, but we're thinking about this every day.
portrait: Vera, 22, is a top mechanical engineering graduate on a one-year graduate contract at a **pump maker** in Zaragoza.
She carries heavy debt, has about ten days of money saved and gets no family help.
She is centrist and resistant, avoids AI tools and distrusts what she doesn't understand.
She would rather ask nothing than seem needy, which leaves her exposed if the **contract** isn't renewed.
She is anxious in most worlds, alarmed in 2028 and only uneasy with ten years to plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, with no savings and no field to go back to.
whatWouldHelp: Real **notice** from companies, plus a government plan that doesn't make people beg for help.
